passages.label: Text 1
passages.text: For decades, ecologists assumed that the loss of large predators mainly affected the animals those predators ate. Research on "trophic cascades" suggests the effects reach much further. After wolves were reintroduced to parts of the western United States, some researchers reported that elk grazed less along streams, allowing willows to recover and riverbanks to stabilize. On this view, a single predator can reshape an entire landscape.

passages.label: Text 2
passages.text: Studies of trophic cascades are compelling, but ecologist Rosa Delgado cautions against crediting predators alone. In several valleys where willows recovered, she notes, elk numbers had also fallen because of hunting and harsh winters, and beavers had become more active. Untangling these overlapping causes, Delgado argues, requires long-term data from sites where only one factor changed.

content.stem: Based on the texts, how would Delgado (Text 2) most likely respond to the researchers' conclusion described in Text 1?

choices.label: A
choices.text: She would argue that the recovery of willows was caused by hunting rather than by wolves.

choices.label: B
choices.text: She would caution that the conclusion may overstate the role of wolves, since other changes happened at the same time.

choices.label: C
choices.text: She would agree that wolves reshaped the landscape but doubt that willows were affected.

choices.label: D
choices.text: She would claim that trophic cascades cannot occur in places where beavers live.

content.explanation: Text 1 concludes that wolves alone reshaped the landscape. Delgado "cautions against crediting predators alone" because hunting, harsh winters and beavers changed at the same time, and she says separating these causes needs better data. She doesn't deny wolves played a role; she says the conclusion may give them too much credit. That is choice B.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: This goes too far. Delgado says the causes are hard to untangle; she doesn't name hunting as the cause instead of wolves.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: Delgado accepts that willows recovered; her point is about what caused the recovery.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: Delgado mentions beavers as one more change to account for, not as something that prevents trophic cascades.

passages.label: Text 1
passages.text: Several rural school districts have switched to a four-day school week, making each remaining day longer. Administrators in these districts report that the change saves money on buses and heating and makes it easier to hire teachers, who value the extra day off. Many see the schedule as an appealing option for small districts with tight budgets.

passages.label: Text 2
passages.text: Education researcher Kendra Sloane acknowledges that four-day weeks can cut costs. But in her analysis of districts that adopted the schedule, students' math scores grew more slowly than in similar districts that kept five-day weeks. Sloane argues that districts should weigh the savings against these academic effects before switching.

content.stem: Based on the texts, how would Sloane (Text 2) most likely respond to the administrators' view described in Text 1?

choices.label: A
choices.text: She would dispute their claim that a four-day week saves money.

choices.label: B
choices.text: She would argue that hiring teachers is a more important goal than saving money.

choices.label: C
choices.text: She would urge every district with a tight budget to adopt the schedule.

choices.label: D
choices.text: She would agree that the schedule can save money but caution that it may slow students' learning.

content.explanation: Sloane "acknowledges that four-day weeks can cut costs," so she agrees with the administrators on savings. But she found slower growth in math scores and says the savings should be weighed against that. Choice D captures both parts.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: Sloane explicitly accepts that the schedule can cut costs.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: Sloane doesn't discuss teacher hiring at all; her concern is student achievement.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: Sloane urges caution, not adoption, because of the effects on math scores.

passages.label: Text 1
passages.text: Over the past fifty years, many ensembles have begun performing music from the 1700s on instruments built as they were at the time, such as violins strung with gut rather than steel. Critic Martin Ehrlich praises this approach, arguing that only period instruments let listeners hear the music as its composers intended it to sound.

passages.label: Text 2
passages.text: Musicologist Ayesha Grant points out that composers of the 1700s often rearranged their own works for whatever instruments were available, replacing a violin with a flute when needed. To Grant, this suggests that these composers cared less about exact sounds than modern purists assume, and that performances on modern instruments can be just as faithful to their intentions.

content.stem: Based on the texts, how would Grant (Text 2) most likely respond to Ehrlich's argument in Text 1?

choices.label: A
choices.text: She would say it assumes that composers were more attached to particular instrument sounds than they actually were.

choices.label: B
choices.text: She would agree that period instruments are the only faithful way to perform this music.

choices.label: C
choices.text: She would argue that modern audiences dislike the sound of gut strings.

choices.label: D
choices.text: She would claim that composers of the 1700s never wrote music for specific instruments.

content.explanation: Ehrlich's argument depends on the idea that composers intended a specific sound that only period instruments can produce. Grant notes that composers freely swapped instruments, which suggests they cared less about exact sounds. So she would say Ehrlich's argument overstates how attached composers were to particular sounds (choice A).

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: Grant says modern instruments "can be just as faithful," so she would not agree that period instruments are the only faithful option.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: Grant says nothing about what modern audiences like.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: This goes too far. Grant says composers often rearranged works, not that they never wrote for specific instruments.

passages.label: Text 1
passages.text: Green roofs, which are covered with soil and plants, are increasingly popular in cities. In one city, office buildings with green roofs used noticeably less energy for summer air-conditioning than similar buildings with ordinary roofs. Supporters say every city should require green roofs on all new buildings.

passages.label: Text 2
passages.text: Engineer Tomasz Wilk notes that green roofs perform best where summers are hot and rain falls regularly. In dry climates, the plants need frequent watering, which can cancel out the savings, and in cool climates the cooling benefit is small. Wilk recommends that cities study their local conditions before adopting any rules.

content.stem: Based on the texts, how would Wilk (Text 2) most likely respond to the supporters' proposal in Text 1?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He would argue that green roofs never reduce energy use.

choices.label: B
choices.text: He would say that one requirement for every city ignores how much the results depend on local climate.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He would claim that the study of office buildings measured energy use incorrectly.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He would recommend requiring green roofs only on office buildings.

content.explanation: The supporters want every city to require green roofs. Wilk says the benefits depend on climate: they shrink in dry or cool places, so cities should study local conditions first. He would object that a single rule for all cities overlooks those differences (choice B).

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: Wilk says green roofs "perform best" in some climates, so he doesn't think they never help.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: Wilk doesn't question how the study was done; he questions applying it everywhere.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: Wilk's concern is climate, not building type.

passages.label: Text 1
passages.text: Popular accounts often present major inventions as the work of lone geniuses. In this telling, Thomas Edison invented the electric light bulb in 1879 through sheer persistence, testing material after material until he found one that worked. Such stories are inspiring, and they reflect a widespread belief that progress depends on exceptional individuals.

passages.label: Text 2
passages.text: Historians of technology tell a more crowded story. Inventors including Joseph Swan in England had built working incandescent lamps before Edison did. Edison's team improved on these designs, producing a longer-lasting bulb, and developed a system of generators and wiring to power it. Invention, in this view, is usually cumulative and collaborative.

content.stem: Based on the texts, how would the historians described in Text 2 most likely respond to the popular accounts in Text 1?

choices.label: A
choices.text: By agreeing that Edison's persistence was the main reason electric lighting succeeded

choices.label: B
choices.text: By arguing that Joseph Swan, not Edison, deserves to be remembered as the lone genius behind the light bulb

choices.label: C
choices.text: By arguing that crediting Edison alone overlooks earlier inventors and the work of his team

choices.label: D
choices.text: By denying that Edison made any real contribution to electric lighting

content.explanation: Text 1 describes accounts that credit Edison alone. Text 2 says other inventors built lamps first and that Edison's team improved them and built a power system, so invention is "cumulative and collaborative." The historians would say the lone-genius story leaves out these other contributors (choice C).

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: Text 2 doesn't single out Edison's persistence; it stresses earlier inventors and teamwork.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: Text 2 rejects the lone-genius idea altogether, so replacing Edison with Swan would contradict its point.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: Text 2 credits Edison's team with a longer-lasting bulb and a power system, so it doesn't deny his contribution.

passages.label: Text 1
passages.text: When a travel company let half of its customer-service staff work from home for nine months, economist Rafael Ortiz found that the remote employees handled about 10 percent more calls per day than those who stayed in the office. Ortiz concludes that working from home makes employees more productive.

passages.label: Text 2
passages.text: Studies of remote work often measure productivity by counting tasks that are easy to count, such as calls answered. Management scholar Yuki Tanabe argues that much valuable work, such as mentoring new colleagues or trading ideas that lead to new products, happens in informal conversations and never shows up in such tallies. Conclusions based only on countable output, she warns, may miss what remote work costs.

content.stem: Based on the texts, how would Tanabe (Text 2) most likely respond to Ortiz's conclusion in Text 1?

choices.label: A
choices.text: She would claim that the remote employees actually answered fewer calls than the office employees.

choices.label: B
choices.text: She would say the conclusion rests on a narrow measure that may leave out valuable work that is hard to count.

choices.label: C
choices.text: She would argue that customer-service jobs should never be done from home.

choices.label: D
choices.text: She would agree with the conclusion and add that remote work also improves mentoring.

content.explanation: Ortiz measured productivity by calls handled. Tanabe warns that conclusions based only on countable output like "calls answered" can miss informal work such as mentoring and sharing ideas. She would say his conclusion relies on too narrow a measure (choice B).

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: Tanabe doesn't dispute the call counts; she questions what they leave out.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: Tanabe warns that some costs may be missed but doesn't say any job must be done in an office.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: Tanabe suggests mentoring is the kind of work remote studies may miss, implying it may suffer, not improve.

passages.label: Text 1
passages.text: Readers of novelist Ilse Moravec often remark on her spare style: short sentences, few adjectives and almost no description of what her characters feel. Critic Paul Danner argues that this restraint leaves her novels emotionally cold, keeping readers at a distance from characters they are never allowed to know.

passages.label: Text 2
passages.text: Critic Noor Haddad finds Moravec's restraint anything but cold. Because her characters rarely name their feelings, readers must infer grief or longing from small gestures: a coat left on a chair, a letter never answered. Haddad contends that this effort draws readers more deeply into the characters' inner lives than direct statement could.

content.stem: Based on the texts, how would Haddad (Text 2) most likely respond to Danner's claim in Text 1?

choices.label: A
choices.text: She would dispute that Moravec's writing is restrained.

choices.label: B
choices.text: She would agree that the novels are emotionally cold but argue that the coldness is intentional.

choices.label: C
choices.text: She would point out that Moravec's characters often describe their feelings directly.

choices.label: D
choices.text: She would argue that the restraint Danner describes actually increases readers' engagement with the characters' emotions.

content.explanation: Both critics agree that Moravec rarely describes her characters' feelings. Danner thinks this keeps readers at a distance; Haddad thinks the effort of inferring feelings draws readers "more deeply into the characters' inner lives." So she would argue the same restraint has the opposite effect from the one Danner claims (choice D).

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: Haddad accepts that the style is restrained; she disagrees about its effect.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: Haddad says the restraint is "anything but cold," so she wouldn't agree that the novels are cold.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: Haddad says the characters "rarely name their feelings," which contradicts this choice.

passages.label: Text 1
passages.text: Because feathers are essential to flight in modern birds, scientists long assumed that feathers first evolved to help the ancestors of birds fly. On this view, feathers were an adaptation for gliding or flapping from their very beginning.

passages.label: Text 2
passages.text: Since the 1990s, paleontologists have described many dinosaurs that had simple, hairlike feathers but could not fly, such as Sinosauropteryx, a small predator with short arms. These finds suggest that feathers appeared well before flight, perhaps for warmth or display, and were only later put to use in flying.

content.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the assumption described in Text 1?

choices.label: A
choices.text: By arguing that fossil evidence indicates feathers first served other purposes and were later adapted for flight

choices.label: B
choices.text: By arguing that feathers are not actually necessary for flight in modern birds

choices.label: C
choices.text: By suggesting that Sinosauropteryx used its feathers to glide

choices.label: D
choices.text: By agreeing that feathers evolved for flight but questioning when that happened

content.explanation: Text 1 describes the assumption that feathers evolved for flight from the start. Text 2 cites feathered dinosaurs that couldn't fly and concludes that feathers came first, perhaps for warmth or display, and were "only later put to use in flying." Choice A states that response.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: Text 2 says nothing to challenge the role of feathers in modern birds' flight.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: Text 2 presents Sinosauropteryx as a dinosaur that could not fly.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: Text 2 rejects the idea that feathers evolved for flight, not just its timing.

passages.label: Text 1
passages.text: Urban planner Celia Novak compared fifty cities and found that those with the most kilometers of protected bike lanes also had the highest shares of residents who commute by bicycle. Novak concludes that building protected lanes leads more people to cycle, and she urges cities to expand their networks.

passages.label: Text 2
passages.text: Transportation researcher Idris Mensah notes that cities often build bike lanes in response to demand: where many people already cycle, officials face pressure to add lanes. A comparison of cities at a single moment therefore can't show which came first. Mensah points instead to cities that built large networks within a few years; cycling rose sharply afterward in several of them, which he considers far stronger evidence that lanes increase cycling.

content.stem: Based on the texts, how would Mensah (Text 2) most likely respond to Novak's conclusion in Text 1?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He would reject it, arguing that bike lanes are built only where many people already cycle.

choices.label: B
choices.text: He would accept the conclusion but argue that her comparison of cities does not, on its own, establish it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He would argue that her finding is better explained by differences in the cities' sizes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He would agree with it and consider her comparison the strongest available evidence for it.

content.explanation: Mensah believes lanes do increase cycling; he cites cities where cycling rose after large networks were built. But he argues that a single-moment comparison like Novak's "can't show which came first," because cities also build lanes where people already cycle. So he would accept her conclusion while saying her evidence alone doesn't prove it (choice B).

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: Mensah says cities "often" build lanes in response to demand, not "only," and he thinks lanes do increase cycling, so he wouldn't reject the conclusion.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: Mensah never mentions city size; his concern is which came first, the lanes or the cyclists.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: Mensah agrees with the conclusion but considers the before-and-after evidence far stronger than a single-moment comparison.

passages.label: Text 1
passages.text: Vervet monkeys give different alarm calls for leopards, eagles and snakes, and each call triggers a different response: monkeys hearing the leopard call run up into trees, while those hearing the eagle call look up or dive into bushes. Because each call corresponds to a specific kind of predator, some researchers argue that the calls function much like words, naming the danger.

passages.label: Text 2
passages.text: Animal behaviorist Selin Arslan agrees that vervet alarm calls are remarkably specific but questions what they are specific about. Each predator requires a different escape, she observes, so a call could just as well mean "climb!" or "hide!" as "leopard" or "eagle." Arslan argues that the monkeys' responses alone cannot tell these possibilities apart.

content.stem: Based on the texts, how would Arslan (Text 2) most likely respond to the argument in Text 1 that the calls function like words naming dangers?

choices.label: A
choices.text: She would argue that the calls are not specific enough to distinguish one predator from another.

choices.label: B
choices.text: She would argue that vervet monkeys respond to every alarm call in the same way.

choices.label: C
choices.text: She would argue that the monkeys' reactions are equally consistent with the calls being instructions about how to escape.

choices.label: D
choices.text: She would argue that the calls name predators but give no indication of what the monkeys should do.

content.explanation: Text 1 reasons that because each call matches a predator and triggers a matching response, the call names the predator. Arslan accepts that the calls are specific, but notes that each predator also requires a different escape, so a call could mean "climb!" rather than "leopard." She says the responses can't tell these apart. Choice C states this.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: Arslan says the calls are "remarkably specific," so she doesn't think they fail to distinguish predators.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: Both texts describe different responses to different calls.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: Arslan raises the possibility that the calls are instructions, not that they are names; she doesn't conclude that they name predators.

passages.label: Text 1
passages.text: Many art museums now allow visitors to photograph the works on display. Curators at one museum report that since lifting their ban on cameras, visitors have stayed longer and shared thousands of images of the collection online. The curators see photography as a way to deepen visitors' engagement with art.

passages.label: Text 2
passages.text: Psychologist Hannah Odum asked museum visitors either to photograph a set of paintings or simply to look at them. The next day, those who had taken photos remembered fewer details of the paintings than those who had only looked. Odum suggests that relying on a camera may lead people to pay less attention to what is in front of them.

content.stem: Based on the texts, how would Odum (Text 2) most likely respond to the curators' view described in Text 1?

choices.label: A
choices.text: She would agree that photography deepens engagement, since visitors who take photos stay in museums longer.

choices.label: B
choices.text: She would question whether photographing artworks truly deepens engagement, since it may reduce how closely visitors look at the art.

choices.label: C
choices.text: She would argue that museums should forbid visitors from sharing images of artworks online.

choices.label: D
choices.text: She would claim that visitors who take photographs leave museums sooner than those who don't.

content.explanation: The curators think photography deepens engagement. Odum found that people who photographed paintings remembered fewer details, and she suggests cameras may make people pay less attention. Her finding gives reason to doubt that photography deepens engagement with the art itself. Choice B is correct.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: Odum's study points the other way: photographing paintings was linked to remembering less about them. She doesn't discuss how long visitors stay.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: Odum says nothing about sharing images online or about what museums should forbid.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: Odum's study measured memory, not time spent in the museum, and Text 1 reports that visitors stayed longer.

passages.label: Text 1
passages.text: City forester Dale Morrow recommends that all new street trees in his city be silver lindens. A uniform canopy, he argues, gives streets a tidy appearance, and buying trees in bulk from one nursery lowers costs. Maintenance is simpler too, since crews need to learn the care of only one kind of tree.

passages.label: Text 2
passages.text: In the early twentieth century, American cities lined countless streets with elms. When Dutch elm disease spread across the country from the 1930s onward, it killed most of them, leaving many neighborhoods nearly bare. Ecologists now urge cities to plant a mix of species so that no single pest or disease can strip a city of its trees.

content.stem: Based on the texts, how would the ecologists described in Text 2 most likely respond to Morrow's recommendation in Text 1?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They would support it, since silver lindens are not affected by Dutch elm disease.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They would accept it as long as the city bought its lindens from several different nurseries.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They would recommend that the city plant elms instead of silver lindens.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They would warn that planting a single species leaves the city's trees vulnerable to being wiped out by one pest or disease.

content.explanation: Text 2 uses the elms as a warning: when a city plants mostly one species, a single disease can kill most of its trees. That is why the ecologists urge a mix of species. Morrow recommends planting only one species, so the ecologists would warn that his plan carries the same risk. Choice D is correct.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: The elm example is a warning about relying on any one species. Lindens could face their own pest or disease, which is exactly the ecologists' concern.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: The ecologists' concern is a variety of species, not a variety of suppliers. Lindens from several nurseries would still be one species.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: Text 2 presents elms as the example of what went wrong; the ecologists would not recommend replacing one single species with another.

passages.label: Text 1
passages.text: When an author revises a novel late in life, editors must choose which version to print. Scholar Alan Pryce argues that the final revision should be treated as definitive: it represents the author's most considered judgment, and printing an earlier version risks giving readers a draft the author had rejected.

passages.label: Text 2
passages.text: Textual scholar Mira Castellanos observes that authors who revise decades later are often, in effect, different writers, with new concerns and a new audience. A late revision, she argues, is less a corrected copy of the original than a new work in its own right, and the original version, which readers first encountered and responded to, deserves to be read on its own terms.

content.stem: Based on the texts, how would Castellanos (Text 2) most likely respond to Pryce's claim that an earlier version is a draft the author had rejected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: She would argue that the earlier version is not simply a rejected draft but a distinct work with value of its own.

choices.label: B
choices.text: She would agree that the final revision reflects the author's best judgment and should therefore replace the earlier version.

choices.label: C
choices.text: She would argue that editors should combine the strongest passages of both versions into a single text.

choices.label: D
choices.text: She would point out that authors seldom revise their novels after they have been published.

content.explanation: Pryce treats the earlier version as a draft the author rejected. Castellanos sees a late revision as "a new work in its own right" by an author who has, in effect, become a different writer, and she says the original "deserves to be read on its own terms." So she would reject the idea that the original is merely a rejected draft. Choice A is correct.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: Castellanos says the original deserves to be read on its own terms, so she would not want the revision to replace it.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: Castellanos never suggests merging versions; she treats them as separate works.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: Castellanos's argument assumes that authors do revise, sometimes decades later. She doesn't claim revision is rare.

passages.label: Text 1
passages.text: When the regional transit agency raised fares by 10 percent, ridership fell by only about 3 percent over the following six months. Economist Gareth Lowe concludes that riders are largely insensitive to price, so modest fare increases are a reliable way to raise revenue without losing many passengers.

passages.label: Text 2
passages.text: Transportation analyst Sun-hee Park cautions that travel habits change slowly. A commuter facing higher fares may keep riding at first but, over the next few years, buy a car, change jobs or move. Park's review of fare increases in several cities found that ridership losses typically kept growing for years after a fare hike.

content.stem: Based on the texts, how would Park (Text 2) most likely respond to Lowe's conclusion in Text 1?

choices.label: A
choices.text: She would agree with it, since a 3 percent drop in ridership is small.

choices.label: B
choices.text: She would argue that the agency should lower fares to attract new riders.

choices.label: C
choices.text: She would argue that six months is too short a period to show the full effect of the fare increase on ridership.

choices.label: D
choices.text: She would claim that the fare increase did not reduce ridership at all.

content.explanation: Lowe based his conclusion on the six months after the fare increase. Park found that ridership losses "kept growing for years" after fare hikes, because people change habits slowly. So she would say six months of data can't show the full effect, and the small early drop may underestimate the eventual loss. Choice C is correct.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: Park's point is that early drops understate long-term losses, so the small 3 percent figure wouldn't convince her.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: Park doesn't recommend lowering fares; she discusses only how to measure the effect of raising them.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: Park's view is that fare increases reduce ridership more than they first seem to, not that they have no effect.

passages.label: Text 1
passages.text: Supporters of sending astronauts to Mars argue that human explorers would accomplish far more than robots. A geologist on the surface could spot an unusual rock at a glance, decide on the spot to study it, and collect samples within minutes, work that takes a rover days of careful commands sent from Earth.

passages.label: Text 2
passages.text: Engineer Lucia Ferrante points out that a crewed mission to Mars would cost many times more than a robotic one, largely because astronauts need food, water, air and a way to get home. For the price of a single crewed mission, she argues, space agencies could send dozens of rovers to sites across the planet.

content.stem: Based on the texts, how would Ferrante (Text 2) most likely respond to the supporters' argument in Text 1?

choices.label: A
choices.text: She would respond that whatever astronauts could accomplish, the same money could pay for many robotic missions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: She would claim that rovers can recognize unusual rocks faster than human geologists can.

choices.label: C
choices.text: She would argue that no missions of any kind should be sent to Mars.

choices.label: D
choices.text: She would agree that a crewed mission is the best use of space agencies' budgets.

content.explanation: The supporters argue that a human explorer can do more than a robot. Ferrante doesn't dispute what an astronaut can do; she focuses on cost: one crewed mission costs as much as dozens of rovers. So she would answer that the money for astronauts could fund many robotic missions instead. Choice A is correct.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: Ferrante makes no claim about how quickly rovers recognize rocks; her argument is about cost.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: Ferrante favors sending dozens of rovers, so she clearly supports some missions to Mars.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: Ferrante argues that the money for one crewed mission could pay for dozens of rovers, which suggests she does not see a crewed mission as the best use of the budget.

passages.label: Text 1
passages.text: Great tits living in noisy cities sing at higher pitches than great tits in quiet forests. Biologist Ewa Nowak argues that city birds deliberately shift their songs upward to rise above traffic noise, which is concentrated at low pitches. On this view, the higher pitch is a strategy: the birds choose the notes most likely to be heard.

passages.label: Text 2
passages.text: Researchers studying the Lombard effect, the tendency of animals to call more loudly in noisy settings, note that in many bird species, singing louder automatically raises a song's pitch. If so, the higher songs of city birds may simply be a side effect of their singing more loudly, rather than a separate adjustment aimed at avoiding low-pitched noise.

content.stem: Based on the texts, how would the researchers described in Text 2 most likely respond to Nowak's argument in Text 1?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They would deny that city birds sing at higher pitches than forest birds do.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They would argue that traffic noise has no effect on how birds sing.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They would suggest that the higher pitch may not be a strategy at all but a byproduct of birds singing louder in response to noise.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They would agree with it, since singing louder and singing higher are both ways of choosing the notes most likely to be heard.

content.explanation: Nowak claims the higher pitch is a deliberate strategy to avoid low-pitched traffic noise. The Text 2 researchers accept that city birds sing higher, but they note that singing louder automatically raises pitch. So the higher pitch might be "simply a side effect" of singing louder, not a separate choice. Choice C is correct.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: Text 2 accepts that city birds' songs are higher ("the higher songs of city birds"); it disputes only the reason.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: Text 2 says noise makes birds sing louder, so it agrees that noise affects birdsong.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: Text 2 separates the two: louder singing is the response to noise, and the higher pitch may follow automatically rather than being chosen. That undercuts Nowak's idea of a deliberate strategy.

passages.label: Text 1
passages.text: Lake sediments from the Yucatán Peninsula record a series of severe droughts between about 800 and 1000 CE, the same period in which many Classic Maya cities in the southern lowlands were abandoned. Some researchers conclude that drought was the main cause of this collapse, as failing harvests left cities unable to feed their people.

passages.label: Text 2
passages.text: Archaeologists studying inscriptions point out that warfare among Maya city-states intensified in the decades before many cities were abandoned, and that some cities, including Chichén Itzá in the north, flourished during these same droughts. In their view, drought may have added pressure, but political conflict did much to determine which cities fell.

content.stem: Based on the texts, how would the archaeologists described in Text 2 most likely respond to the conclusion in Text 1?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They would deny that severe droughts occurred in the region between 800 and 1000 CE.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They would argue that drought alone cannot explain the collapse, since some cities thrived during the droughts and warfare was also intensifying.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They would agree that drought was the main cause, since the droughts and the abandonment of cities happened at the same time.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They would argue that the northern cities were abandoned before the southern ones.

content.explanation: Text 1 concludes that drought was the main cause of the collapse. The Text 2 archaeologists accept that drought "may have added pressure," but they point to two problems: warfare was increasing before the abandonments, and some cities, such as Chichén Itzá, flourished during the same droughts. So they would say drought alone can't explain which cities collapsed. Choice B is correct.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: Text 2 refers to "these same droughts" and says drought may have added pressure, so the archaeologists accept that the droughts happened.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: Text 2 gives evidence against drought being the main cause, emphasizing political conflict instead.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: Text 2 says Chichén Itzá in the north flourished during this period; it never says northern cities were abandoned first.

passages.label: Text 1
passages.text: Principal Gloria Haynes opposes moving her high school's start time from 7:30 to 8:30 a.m. A later start, she notes, would mean a later dismissal, cutting into practice time for sports teams and forcing the district to redraw bus routes it shares with the elementary schools.

passages.label: Text 2
passages.text: Sleep researcher Marcus Bell has studied high schools that moved their start times later. Students at these schools slept more, missed fewer days of class and earned slightly higher grades. Bell acknowledges that such changes create real scheduling problems but notes that the districts he studied found ways to solve them.

content.stem: Based on the texts, how would Bell (Text 2) most likely respond to Haynes's position in Text 1?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He would agree that the scheduling problems make a later start time impractical.

choices.label: B
choices.text: He would argue that schools should stop offering after-school sports.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He would deny that a later start time affects bus schedules.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He would acknowledge her concerns but argue that the benefits to students make solving these problems worthwhile.

content.explanation: Haynes opposes a later start because of scheduling problems (sports practice, bus routes). Bell "acknowledges" that such problems are real, but he found that students slept more, attended more and earned better grades, and that districts managed to solve the problems. So he would grant her concerns while arguing the change is worth it. Choice D is correct.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: Bell notes that districts found ways to solve the scheduling problems, so he would not consider them a reason to reject the change.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: Bell never suggests ending sports; he says scheduling problems can be solved.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: Bell acknowledges that later start times create "real scheduling problems," so he would not deny their effects.

passages.label: Text 1
passages.text: Architect Rolf Engel argues that decoration on buildings is a wasteful holdover from the past. A building's beauty, he insists, should come from its proportions and materials alone; carved trim, patterned brickwork and other ornament add cost without improving how a building serves the people who use it.

passages.label: Text 2
passages.text: Environmental psychologist Dana Whitfield showed volunteers photographs of city streets and later asked them to recall routes along them. Volunteers retraced routes more accurately along streets with distinctive, ornamented facades than along streets of plain, similar buildings. Whitfield concludes that ornament can serve a practical purpose: it gives places identities that help people remember and navigate them.

content.stem: Based on the texts, how would Whitfield (Text 2) most likely respond to Engel's claim that ornament does not improve how a building serves its users?

choices.label: A
choices.text: She would argue that ornament can serve people in a practical way by helping them recognize places and find their way.

choices.label: B
choices.text: She would agree that ornament adds cost but argue that cost doesn't matter in architecture.

choices.label: C
choices.text: She would agree that proportions and materials matter more to people than ornament does.

choices.label: D
choices.text: She would claim that plain buildings cost more to construct than ornamented ones.

content.explanation: Engel claims ornament does nothing to help a building's users. Whitfield found that people navigated more accurately along ornamented streets and concluded that ornament "can serve a practical purpose" by making places memorable. That directly answers Engel's claim. Choice A is correct.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: Whitfield doesn't discuss cost at all; her point is that ornament has a practical benefit.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: Whitfield's study doesn't compare ornament with proportions and materials, and her finding favors ornament's usefulness.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: Whitfield makes no claim about construction costs.

passages.label: Text 1
passages.text: In a study of 60 children, psychologist Arjun Mehta found that those who spoke two languages outperformed those who spoke one on tasks requiring rapid switching between rules, such as sorting cards first by color and then by shape. Mehta concludes that managing two languages strengthens the mental skills involved in shifting attention.

passages.label: Text 2
passages.text: Researcher Ingrid Solberg reviewed dozens of studies comparing bilingual and monolingual speakers on attention tasks. Studies reporting an advantage for bilingual speakers, she found, were far more likely to be published than studies of similar size that found no difference, many of which were only presented at conferences. Once those unpublished studies were included, the apparent advantage largely disappeared.

content.stem: Based on the texts, how would Solberg (Text 2) most likely respond to Mehta's conclusion in Text 1?

choices.label: A
choices.text: She would argue that card-sorting tasks do not measure the ability to shift attention.

choices.label: B
choices.text: She would caution that one study's finding of an advantage should be weighed against the broader evidence, which suggests the advantage may be small or absent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: She would argue that bilingual children perform worse than monolingual children on attention tasks.

choices.label: D
choices.text: She would accept Mehta's conclusion, since a published study meets standards that conference presentations do not.

content.explanation: Mehta draws a general conclusion from one study that found a bilingual advantage. Solberg found that such positive studies get published more often than studies finding no difference, and that when all studies are counted, the advantage "largely disappeared." So she would warn that a single positive study can give a misleading picture and should be judged against the full body of evidence. Choice B is correct.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: Solberg doesn't criticize the tasks used to measure attention; her concern is which studies get published.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: Solberg found that the advantage largely disappeared, meaning little or no difference, not that bilingual speakers do worse.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: Solberg's point is that publication favors studies that find an advantage, so a published study finding one is not, on its own, convincing to her.
